- [Observability overview](/observability/overview) — alarms, issues, and notifications in depth

title: Console Overview
content: ## FAQ

title: Console Overview
headingPath: Do I need the Console to use Stacktape?
content:
### Do I need the Console to use Stacktape?

No. [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys) let you authenticate with Stacktape from the CLI or CI/CD pipelines, and `stacktape deploy` does the actual deploying. The Console is the management layer on top — it adds team access, cost visibility, alarms, budgets, issues, guardrails, and the visual config editor. Most teams use both: the CLI (directly or via GitOps) for deploying, and the Console for visibility and operational control.

title: Console Overview
headingPath: Does Stacktape deploy into my own AWS account?
content:
### Does Stacktape deploy into my own AWS account?

Yes. Stacktape uses a cross-account IAM role to manage resources in your AWS account on your behalf, so you never hand over long-lived AWS credentials. Connect more accounts from **AWS Accounts** under the Configuration section. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) for the required role.

title: Console Overview
headingPath: Why aren't my alarm rules firing after I created them?
content:
### Why aren't my alarm rules firing after I created them?

Alarm rules saved in the Console are not live in AWS until the next [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) of each matching stage — that deploy materializes the CloudWatch alarms and EventBridge routing. If you create a rule but don't redeploy, the alarm doesn't exist in AWS yet. The same applies to stack-scoped budget alerts. This design keeps alerts in sync with your deployed infrastructure.

title: Console Overview
headingPath: Why is the Issues page empty even though there are errors in my logs?
content:
### Why is the Issues page empty even though there are errors in my logs?

Issues must be enabled for the relevant projects and stages, and matching stages must be redeployed with CLI 3.8.0 or newer so Stacktape adds the CloudWatch Logs subscription filters. Detection is log-pattern based — it supports TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, and PHP, matching markers like Lambda invoke errors, unhandled promise rejections, exceptions, tracebacks, panics, and stack-trace lines. Errors that don't match those patterns won't be detected. See [Issues](/observability/issues).

title: Console Overview
headingPath: How does Stacktape track AWS costs, and why is the Costs page empty?
content:
### How does Stacktape track AWS costs, and why is the Costs page empty?

The Costs page breaks down AWS costs by project and stage, generated daily from AWS Cost and Usage Reports. New data can take up to a day to appear, so an empty page usually means a recently connected [AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) or that reports haven't propagated yet. See [Managing costs](/managing-costs/overview) for budgets and optimization tips.

title: Console Overview
headingPath: Why is a sidebar item missing for me?
content:
### Why is a sidebar item missing for me?

The Console uses role-based access control, and several sidebar items are permission-gated. Core routes like Overview, Projects, and Activity are always visible, while items such as Users (`members:view`), Costs (`org:view-billing`), Alarms, Guardrails, Secrets, and SSM Params require specific permissions; the Config editor is also hidden for the Viewer role. If a section is missing, ask your organization's owner or admin to adjust your role. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
# Organizations, Projects, and Stages

The Stacktape Console organizes work into three levels: organizations contain projects, and projects contain stages. A project represents a single application — typically one Git repository. A stage is an isolated deployment of that project (such as production, staging, or dev), with its own databases, functions, containers, and networking.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
## How the hierarchy works

The Console structures work in three nested levels. An organization sits at the top and contains projects. Each project contains stages — isolated deployments of that application.

1. **Organization** — groups projects, team members, and settings
2. **Project** — one application, usually one Git repository
3. **Stage** — an isolated deployment (production, staging, dev)

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Organizations

An organization groups related projects, team members, and settings. In the Console, everything you see is scoped to the currently selected organization — projects, costs, alarms, and team settings all belong to the active organization. Switching organizations shows a different set of projects.

Organization-level build runner settings are stored on the organization and include CodeBuild compute type, base image, and additional install commands.

You can manage organizations from the CLI with [`stacktape org:create`](/cli/org-create) and [`stacktape org:list`](/cli/org-list).

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Projects

A Stacktape project represents a single application and usually maps 1:1 to a Git repository. Each project can have multiple stages — fully isolated deployments like `production`, `staging`, or `dev`.

The Projects page lists all projects in the selected organization. Each project card shows:

- **Project name** and connected Git URL (if any)
- **Number of deployed stages** — hovering the stage badge shows counts for alarming alarms, running stages, deployments in progress, errored stages, and not-yet-deployed stages
- **Last deployment time** (displayed as a relative timestamp like "2 hours ago")
- **Current month's cost** with a trend label. When previous-month cost is greater than zero, the label is a percentage change or `Flat`; otherwise it shows `No spend` or `New spend`

Projects are sorted by most recently updated stage, so active projects appear first. A filter input at the top narrows results by project name or Git URL using fuzzy search.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Stages

A stage is a running deployment of a project — a complete, isolated set of AWS resources. Common stage names include `production`, `staging`, `dev`, or `testing`. Stages are fully isolated and do not share resources with each other; examples include containers, functions, databases, and other deployed resources.

To deploy a stage, you need a Stacktape configuration that describes which resources (containers, functions, databases, etc.) to deploy. You can share the same Stacktape configuration across all stages of a project (most common), or maintain separate configurations per stage when environments need different resource shapes.


> **Info:** Stages are sometimes called "environments" in other tools. Stacktape uses "stage" as the canonical term, but they mean the same thing — an isolated deployment of your project. See [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments) for configuration patterns.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content: ## Getting started

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Step 1 — Create a project

In the Console, navigate to **Projects** and click **Create new project**. The menu includes an option to create an empty project. For Git-based automatic deployments, see [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

You can also create a project from the CLI with [`stacktape project:create`](/cli/project-create).

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Step 2 — Create a stage

Inside the project view, click the **New stage** button in the left sidebar to open the stage creation form.

Once a stage is created, clicking it in the sidebar navigates to the deployment setup. If the project has a connected Git repository, the Console routes to `/projects/{project}/create-new-stage/{stage}`. If no Git repository is connected, the Console routes to `/projects/{project}/create-new-stage-using-cli/{stage}` instead.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Step 3 — Deploy

Use [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) for CLI deployment — see that page for required options — or trigger a deployment through [GitOps](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

```bash
stacktape deploy --projectName my-app --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

Once a stage has been deployed, clicking it in the sidebar navigates to that stage's overview route (`/projects/{project}/{stage}/overview`). The project details query refetches every 6 seconds except on the create-new-stage page, so deployment status updates while the page is open.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
## Common tasks

The Console provides shortcuts for day-to-day project management directly from the Projects page and the project overview sidebar.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Filtering and finding projects

On the Projects page, use the filter input to search by project name or Git URL. The fuzzy search narrows results as you type. Projects are sorted by the most recently deployed stage, so active projects appear first. When no projects exist yet, the page displays "No projects created yet." The **Create new project** button remains available in the page header.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Viewing stage details

Click a project card to open the project view. The left sidebar orders entries as: operation-only stages (in-progress or recently failed deployments), saved undeployed stages, deployed stages, and undeployed names without saved records. Dev-mode stacks are sorted after regular deployed stages within the deployed-stage portion. Clicking a deployed stage navigates to that stage's overview route (`/projects/{project}/{stage}/overview`).

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Configuring build runners

Organization-level build runner settings store the CodeBuild compute type, base image, and additional install commands on the selected organization. In the Console, navigate to **Projects**, click the gear icon in the page header, and select **Configure Codebuild settings**. This option is visible only to users with the `org:manage-codebuild-settings` permission.

The settings form lets you configure:

- **CodeBuild compute type** — the machine size used for builds
- **Codebuild base image** — the base image value saved for organization-level CodeBuild settings
- **Additional Codebuild install commands** — organization-level commands saved with the CodeBuild settings

Available compute types:

| Compute type | CPU | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| BUILD_GENERAL1_SMALL | 2 vCPU | 4 GB |
| BUILD_GENERAL1_MEDIUM | 4 vCPU | 8 GB |
| BUILD_GENERAL1_LARGE | 8 vCPU | 16 GB |
| BUILD_GENERAL1_XLARGE | 16 vCPU | 32 GB |
| BUILD_GENERAL1_2XLARGE | 72 vCPU | 144 GB |

For most projects, `BUILD_GENERAL1_SMALL` or `BUILD_GENERAL1_MEDIUM` is sufficient. Use larger sizes for projects with heavy compilation (e.g., large monorepos or native dependencies).

See [Build runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners) for details on runner types and configuration options.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Configuring project settings

From the project view, click the gear icon next to the project name to open the settings dropdown. This menu is visible only to users with the `projects:update-settings` permission. Available options depend on your project setup:

| Setting | When visible | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Configure Git deployments** | Git repository connected | Opens the project's Git deployments page — see [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) for setup |
| **Configure Runner** | Always (within settings dropdown) | Opens the project runner configuration modal |
| **Configure GitHub Actions runner** | Git repository connected | Set up a [self-hosted GitHub Actions runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/self-hosted-github-actions-runners) |
| **Delete project** | User also has `projects:delete` permission | Remove the project from the organization |

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Redeploying a stage

When a redeploy is initiated from the project overview, the Console asks for confirmation of the target commit. After confirmation, the Console navigates to the deployment detail logs page (`/projects/{project}/{stage}/deployment-detail/{invocationId}?tab=logs`) where you can monitor build output. See [Build runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners) for runner configuration.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Deleting a stage or project

Deployed stages are deleted from the CLI with [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) — see that page for exact deletion semantics.

To delete a project, open the project settings dropdown (gear icon next to the project name) and select **Delete project**. The settings dropdown requires the `projects:update-settings` permission, and the **Delete project** option within it is shown only to users who also have the `projects:delete` permission. If the project still has deployed stages, the Console warns that it is advised to delete them before continuing and requires explicit confirmation.


> **Warning:** If a project still has deployed stages when you delete it, the Console warns that it is advised to delete them before continuing and requires explicit confirmation.


Non-deployed stages (created in the Console but never deployed) can be removed directly from the sidebar. This only removes the Console record — no AWS resources are affected because none were created. Failed stage entries can be dismissed from the sidebar; the confirmation says this removes deployment history for that stage.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
## Access control

The Stacktape Console uses roles and permissions to control what team members can do within an organization. Key actions on the Projects and project overview pages are gated by the following permissions:

| Permission | Controls |
|---|---|
| `projects:delete` | Deleting a project (shown inside the project settings dropdown, which requires `projects:update-settings`) |
| `projects:update-settings` | Accessing project settings (Git deployments, runner config, GitHub Actions runner) |
| `deployments:delete-non-production` | Controls delete and dismiss actions on stage entries in the project sidebar |
| `org:manage-codebuild-settings` | Configuring organization-level CodeBuild settings |

Users without the required permission do not see the corresponding UI controls — for example, the project settings gear icon is hidden from users who lack `projects:update-settings`.

For a complete breakdown of roles, how permissions map to roles, and how to invite team members, see [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
## Troubleshooting

Common issues when working with projects and stages in the Console.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Failed stage in the sidebar

If a deployment fails, the stage appears as errored in the sidebar. You can dismiss a failed stage using the context menu on that stage entry. The confirmation says dismissing will remove the deployment history for that stage, then refetches the project and operation lists. If a later deployment succeeds, the stage appears through the normal deployed-stage list.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Non-deployed stages in the sidebar

Stages created in the Console but never deployed appear in the sidebar as not-yet-deployed entries. You can delete these directly from the sidebar. This removes only the Console record — no AWS resources are affected because none were created.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Cost shows $0 for active stage

Cost data comes from AWS Cost and Usage Reports, which are generated daily and may take up to a day to appear. Newly deployed stages may show zero cost until daily report data arrives. When previous-month cost is greater than zero, the trend label shows a percentage change or `Flat`; otherwise it shows `No spend` or `New spend`.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content:
### Git repository not connected

If a project was created without linking a Git repository, the project card shows "Git repository not connected" instead of a Git URL. When a project has a connected Git repository, the project settings dropdown includes a **Configure Git deployments** option. When no Git repository is connected, the Console routes to `/projects/{project}/create-new-stage-using-cli/{stage}` for the stage setup flow.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
content: ## FAQ

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: What is the difference between a project and a stage in Stacktape?
content:
### What is the difference between a project and a stage in Stacktape?

A project represents a single application, usually mapped to one Git repository. A stage is an isolated deployment of that project — like production, staging, or dev. Each project can have multiple stages, and each stage has its own databases, functions, containers, and networking. Think of projects as "what you're building" and stages as "where it's running."

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: Should I use one configuration per project or one per stage?
content:
### Should I use one configuration per project or one per stage?

Most teams share a single Stacktape configuration across all stages — the same `stacktape.ts` deploys to production, staging, and dev. This keeps environments consistent and reduces configuration drift. Use separate configurations per stage only when environments genuinely need different resource shapes (for example, a smaller database instance in dev). See [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments) for patterns.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: Why does my active stage show $0 cost?
content:
### Why does my active stage show $0 cost?

Cost data comes from AWS Cost and Usage Reports, which are generated daily and may take up to a day to appear. A newly deployed stage will show $0/mo until the first daily report arrives, even if it is already running resources. The project card displays the current month's cost alongside a trend label (`No spend`, `New spend`, a percentage change, or `Flat`).

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: What is the difference between a Stacktape organization and an AWS account?
content:
### What is the difference between a Stacktape organization and an AWS account?

A Stacktape organization is a grouping layer for projects, team members, and settings within the Console. An AWS account is where your actual infrastructure runs. You connect one or more AWS accounts to your Stacktape organization so deployments can create resources in those accounts. The two concepts operate at different layers — the organization controls who can do what in the Console, while the AWS account controls where resources are provisioned. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) for setup.

title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: When should I create multiple organizations?
content:
### When should I create multiple organizations?

Create separate organizations when you need distinct team boundaries — for example, separating work between different clients, business units, or teams that should not share projects or settings. Most teams need only one organization. If everyone works on the same set of projects, a single organization with role-based access (see [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control)) is simpler to manage.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
# Team and Access Control

The Stacktape Console Users page controls who has access to your organization and what they can do. Invite team members, assign roles that determine each person's permissions, revoke API keys, and remove members when they leave. The Users page hides row actions when your role lacks the required permissions and disables the Invite new member button when inviting is not allowed.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
## Overview

The Users page displays all human members of your organization in a table with columns for Name, E-mail, Role (color-coded badge), Created, Status, MFA, and an actions column. Internal service accounts are filtered out automatically, so you only see real team members. Admin-role users cannot perform any actions on Owner-role members.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
## Roles and permissions

Every organization member has a role that determines which actions they can perform. The Users page displays each member's role as a color-coded badge. The only role-specific behavioral constraint enforced directly on the Users page is that Admin-role users cannot perform actions on Owner-role members — the edit, revoke-key, and remove buttons are hidden entirely for those rows.

The Users page checks your current permissions before showing action buttons. Four specific permission gates control the actions on this page:

| Permission | Controls |
|-----------|----------|
| `members:invite` | Ability to invite new members |
| `members:remove` | Ability to remove existing members |
| `members:update-role` | Ability to edit a member's role |
| `api-keys:revoke-all` | Ability to revoke all of a member's API keys |

When your role lacks one of these permissions, the corresponding action button does not appear. The Admin-on-Owner constraint is enforced separately — even if an Admin has the `members:update-role` permission, the edit, revoke, and remove buttons are hidden for Owner-role members.


> **Info:** The four permissions above are the action gates visible on the Users page. Your role determines which of these permissions you have.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
## Walkthrough: inviting a team member

Adding a new person to your organization is the most common task on the Users page. Here is how to do it.

1. In the Stacktape Console, navigate to the **Users** page for your organization.
2. Click the **Invite new member** button in the top-right area to open the invite form.
3. Complete the form and submit the invitation.

The new member appears in the Users table with status **Invited** until they confirm their account. Once confirmed, the Users table displays their Cognito-derived account state instead of "Invited."

The **Invite new member** button is disabled in three situations, each with its own tooltip message:

- **Your role lacks the `members:invite` permission** — the tooltip reads "You do not have permission to invite members."
- **You are on a personal organization** — the tooltip explains that personal organizations do not support additional members and directs you to create a named organization.
- **Your organization has reached its member limit** — the tooltip directs you to upgrade your subscription plan.


> **Warning:** You cannot invite members to a personal (default) organization. Personal organizations are limited to a single member. Create a named organization first, then invite your team there.

title: Team and Access Control
content: ## Common tasks

title: Team and Access Control
content:
### Editing a member's role

When your role includes the `members:update-role` permission, an edit button (pencil icon) appears next to eligible members in the Users table. Clicking it opens the update form where you can change the member's role. Admin users do not see the edit button on Owner-role members.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
### Removing a member

When your role includes the `members:remove` permission, a delete button (trash icon) appears next to eligible members. Clicking it opens a confirmation dialog showing the member's name and current role. Confirming immediately removes the member from the organization.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
### Revoking a member's API keys

When your role includes the `api-keys:revoke-all` permission, a key-revoke button appears next to eligible members. The confirmation dialog states: "This will immediately invalidate all their active API keys in this organization." Once confirmed, all of that member's [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys) in the organization are revoked.


> **Tip:** The Users page exposes member removal and API key revocation as separate actions with separate confirmation dialogs. When offboarding a team member, use the revoke action when you want to explicitly invalidate programmatic credentials.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
### Checking member status and MFA

The Users table shows two status-related columns that help you understand each member's account state:

- **Status** — shows "Invited" for members who have not yet confirmed their account. Confirmed members display their Cognito-derived account state: Confirmed, External provider, Reset required, Force change password, Archived, Compromised, or Unknown.
- **MFA** — shows "External" for members authenticated solely through an external identity provider, "Enabled" for members with multi-factor authentication configured, or "Disabled" otherwise. Unconfirmed (invited) members always show "Disabled."

Each member manages their own MFA and password settings. See [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings) for per-user account management.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
## Member limits

The maximum number of members your organization can have depends on its type and subscription plan. The Console computes this limit based on whether the organization is personal and the subscription plan type, then disables the **Invite new member** button when the current member count reaches that maximum.

Personal organizations cannot invite additional members — they are limited to the account owner. For named organizations, the member limit varies by subscription plan. Visit [Billing and Subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) to see your current plan's limits and upgrade options.

title: Team and Access Control
content: ## Troubleshooting

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: "You do not have permission to invite members"
content:
### "You do not have permission to invite members"

Your role does not include the `members:invite` permission. Ask someone with the `members:invite` permission to invite the member for you, or someone with `members:update-role` to change your role.

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: Invite button disabled on a named organization
content:
### Invite button disabled on a named organization

Your organization has reached the maximum member count for its subscription plan. Check [Billing and Subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) to see your current plan and upgrade options.

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: No action buttons visible for a member
content:
### No action buttons visible for a member

Two possible causes: your role lacks the relevant permissions (`members:update-role`, `members:remove`, `api-keys:revoke-all`), or you hold the Admin role and the target member is an Owner. The Users page hides edit, revoke, and remove actions from Admin users on Owner-role rows.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
### Member shows "Invited" status indefinitely

The invited member has not confirmed their account. The invitation email may have been missed or filtered. The Users page does not expose a resend-invitation action from this view.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
### Member shows "External provider" status

This member authenticated through an external identity provider rather than a direct email/password account. Their MFA column shows "External" because authentication — including any second factor — is managed by the external provider.

title: Team and Access Control
content:
## Related features

- [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings) — manage your personal account: name, password, and MFA.
- [API Keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys) — create and manage API keys for CLI and CI/CD authentication.
- [Organizations, Projects, and Stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages) — understand how projects and stages are organized within an organization.
- [Billing and Subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) — manage your subscription plan and member limits.
- [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) — set organization-wide deployment rules.
- [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) — configure automated deployments from your repositories.

title: Team and Access Control
content: ## FAQ

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: Can an Admin remove or edit an Owner?
content:
### Can an Admin remove or edit an Owner?

No. The Users page hides the edit, revoke, and remove buttons entirely from Admin-role users on Owner-role rows. This constraint is enforced in the UI independently of the four permission gates.

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: Is removing a member the same as revoking their API keys?
content:
### Is removing a member the same as revoking their API keys?

No. The Users page exposes them as two independent actions, each with its own confirmation dialog. Removing a member removes them from the organization. Revoking API keys invalidates their programmatic credentials. For a complete offboarding, use both actions — revoke API keys to invalidate programmatic credentials, then remove the member.

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: Can I enforce MFA for all organization members?
content:
### Can I enforce MFA for all organization members?

The Users page displays each member's MFA status but does not offer an organization-wide MFA enforcement toggle. Each member enables MFA individually through their own [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings). Members authenticated via an external identity provider show MFA as "External" because their provider handles authentication.

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: Why is a member stuck on "Invited" status?
content:
### Why is a member stuck on "Invited" status?

The member appears with status "Invited" until they confirm their account; only then does the table show their Cognito-derived state (such as "Confirmed"). If they stay "Invited" indefinitely, the invitation email was likely missed or filtered — and note the Users page does not expose a resend-invitation action from this view. Unconfirmed members always show "Disabled" for MFA until they complete account setup.

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: Why can't I invite members to my organization?
content:
### Why can't I invite members to my organization?

If the **Invite new member** button is disabled, it is one of three reasons, each with its own tooltip: your role lacks the `members:invite` permission, you are on a personal organization (which is limited to a single member — create a named organization instead), or your organization has reached its member limit for the current subscription plan. See [Billing and Subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) for upgrade options.

title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: How do I choose the right role for a team member?
content:
### How do I choose the right role for a team member?

Assign the least-privileged role that lets the member do their job. A member's role determines which of the four permission gates they hold — `members:invite`, `members:remove`, `members:update-role`, and `api-keys:revoke-all` — and an Admin can never edit, remove, or revoke keys for an Owner regardless of permissions. To change a role, click the edit (pencil) button for the member and pick a new role in the update form.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
# Visual Config Editor

The Stacktape Console includes a browser-based config editor for selecting, editing, and saving Stacktape configuration templates. It provides hover documentation and autocompletion shortcuts for Stacktape configuration properties, includes a preset menu, and can start AI config generation from a Git repository — so you can build infrastructure configurations without leaving the browser.


> Screenshot: Stacktape Console's visual config editor showing a Stacktape configuration with autocompletion suggestions for resource properties Caption: The config editor provides hover documentation and autocompletion for Stacktape configuration properties.

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: When to use the config editor
content:
## When to use the config editor

The config editor is most valuable in three scenarios:

- **Getting started with Stacktape** — the editor includes a preset menu and can start AI config generation from a Git repository, so you can get started without writing a config from scratch. You get hover docs and a CloudFormation preview without installing anything locally.
- **Prototyping infrastructure changes** — iterate on config changes in the browser. The CloudFormation template and tree views let you inspect the compiled CloudFormation resources generated from your Stacktape config.
- **Working in the Console** — manage named configuration templates for the selected organization directly in the Console.

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: When NOT to use the config editor
content:
## When NOT to use the config editor

For mature projects where the Stacktape config lives in version control, most teams edit `stacktape.ts` directly in their IDE (VS Code, Cursor, or similar). A local [TypeScript config](/configuration/configuration-files) gives you variables, conditionals, loops, and IDE refactoring tools. The config editor is a tool for working with Console-managed templates, not a replacement for source-controlled configuration.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
## Editor views

The config editor provides three views, each showing a different representation of your configuration.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
### Editor

The main editing view where you write and modify your Stacktape config. Hover over any property to see its documentation. Trigger autocompletion with `Ctrl+Space` on Windows/Linux or `Cmd+Space` on Mac.

The editor also exposes a preset menu for starting from a ready-made configuration.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
### CloudFormation template

A read-only view showing your Stacktape config statically compiled into an AWS CloudFormation template. Use this to inspect the compiled CloudFormation resources generated from your configuration. The template is statically compiled and is not 100% accurate because some information is known only during deployment.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
### Tree view

A hierarchical tree view of the compiled CloudFormation resources. Like the CloudFormation template view, this representation is not 100% accurate because some information is known only during deployment. The tree view is useful for navigating large configurations and understanding the relationships between compiled resources without reading raw CloudFormation JSON.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
## Templates

The config editor page includes a template selector for choosing which saved template to load into the editor. Selecting a template loads its content into the editor, where you can modify and save it. Saving updates that template for the selected organization.


> **Info:** Templates marked as created in the Console for a new stage are read-only in the config editor. The editor displays: "This config can only be edited on the stage configuration page" with a link to that page.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
## AI config generation

The config editor can start AI config generation from a selected public or private Git repository and branch. See [AI config generation](/using-with-ai/config-generation-from-repository) for details on how the repository analysis works.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
### Starting a generation

Open the AI generation dialog in the editor. To start AI config generation, choose a repository type, provide or select a repository, choose a branch, then start generation:

1. **Choose repository type** — **Private** or **Public**.
   - **Private**: select a repository from your connected Git provider installations. The repository dropdown lists all repositories accessible through your connected providers. If no repositories appear, the dropdown shows "No repositories available" (when you have installations but none match) or "You need to connect a Git provider first" (when no providers are connected). The editor provides a "Connect new Git provider" link to set up a [Git provider integration](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).
   - **Public**: paste a public Git repository URL into the "Repository URL" field.
2. **Select a branch**. The editor auto-selects the default branch when available. You can choose a different branch from the dropdown.
3. **Start generation**. The start control is disabled until both a repository and branch are selected. The configured disabled text is: "Please select Git repository and branch to generate config from." The editor passes a cleanup callback that deletes the temporary AI-generation project.

The editor starts AI config generation for the selected repository and branch. See [AI config generation](/using-with-ai/config-generation-from-repository) for details on the generation process and reviewing the result.


> **Warning:** AI-generated configs are a starting point, not a finished product. Always review the generated resources, packaging paths, and environment variables before deploying.

title: Visual Config Editor
content: ## Common tasks

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
### Saving changes

When you modify the config, save your changes to persist them to the current template. Saving updates the template content for the selected organization.

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: Using the config in a project
content:
### Using the config in a project

When moving to a local project, create a `stacktape.ts` file (recommended) or `stacktape.yaml` in your project, then run [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) to deploy your stack, or set up [GitOps](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) for automatic deployments on push. Use [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) when you're starting a new local project.

title: Visual Config Editor
content: ## Troubleshooting

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
### Autocompletion not appearing

Trigger autocompletion with `Ctrl+Space` on Windows/Linux or `Cmd+Space` on Mac.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
### CloudFormation preview shows approximate values

The CloudFormation template view is a static compilation. It is not 100% accurate because some information is known only during deployment. This is expected behavior — the actual deployed template resolves all values at deploy time.

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: Config linked to a stage is read-only
content:
### Config linked to a stage is read-only

Templates marked as created in the Console for a new stage are read-only in the config editor. The editor links to the stage's configuration page where you can make edits.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
### AI generation button is disabled

The generation button requires both a repository and a branch to be selected before you can start. For private repositories, you also need at least one connected Git provider installation. If the repository dropdown shows "No repositories available" or "You need to connect a Git provider first", use the "Connect new Git provider" link in the editor to set up a [Git provider integration](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: No repositories available for AI generation
content:
### No repositories available for AI generation

For private repository generation, the editor pulls repositories from your connected Git provider installations. If the dropdown is empty despite having installations, check that the installation has access to the repository you need. The editor shows how many Git provider installations you have and provides a link to connect additional providers.

title: Visual Config Editor
content:
## Related features

- [Configuration files](/configuration/configuration-files) — TypeScript and YAML config formats and the `defineConfig` pattern.
- [AI config generation](/using-with-ai/config-generation-from-repository) — Deep dive into how the AI generator analyzes your repository.
- [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) — Auto-deploy configs when you push to your repository.
- [Organizations, projects, and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages) — How projects and stages relate to configs.
- [Secrets](/configuration/secrets) — Reference secrets in your config with the `$Secret()` directive.
- [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) — Use `connectTo` to wire resources together.

title: Visual Config Editor
content: ## FAQ

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: Should I use the visual config editor or my local IDE?
content:
### Should I use the visual config editor or my local IDE?

Both work well at different stages. The config editor is convenient when you want to draft a config in the Console — for example, when starting from a preset or generating one from a Git repository. Once your project's config lives in version control, most teams edit `stacktape.ts` directly in their IDE using the [TypeScript config](/configuration/configuration-files) format, which gives you variables, conditionals, loops, and IDE refactoring tools.

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: Can I generate a config from a private repository?
content:
### Can I generate a config from a private repository?

Yes. Choose the **Private** repository type in the AI generation dialog. The dropdown lists repositories from your connected Git provider installations. If no repositories appear, you need to connect a Git provider first — the editor provides a "Connect new Git provider" link to set up a [Git provider integration](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: What is the difference between templates and config files?
content:
### What is the difference between templates and config files?

Templates are named Stacktape configurations stored in the Console and edited in the visual config editor. A local project config file is either `stacktape.ts` or `stacktape.yaml`, used by the [CLI](/cli/deploy) for deployments. [GitOps](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) is another deployment option that works from your repository. To move from a template to a deployable project, use the template content in a Stacktape config file in your project.

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: Is the CloudFormation preview the exact template that gets deployed?
content:
### Is the CloudFormation preview the exact template that gets deployed?

The CloudFormation preview is a static approximation. It shows what AWS resources Stacktape creates from your configuration, but it is not 100% accurate because some information is known only during deployment. The preview is useful for understanding your stack's structure before deployment, but the exact template used during deployment resolves all dynamic values.

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: Can I edit a stage-linked config in the editor?
content:
### Can I edit a stage-linked config in the editor?

No — templates marked as created in the Console for a new stage are read-only in the config editor. The editor links to the stage's configuration page where you can make edits. See [organizations, projects, and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages) for more on how stages relate to configs.

title: Visual Config Editor
headingPath: What happens if AI config generation fails?
content:
### What happens if AI config generation fails?

If initialization fails, the Console shows "Failed to initialize AI config generation." The generation runs in a temporary Console project that is cleaned up automatically afterward, so a failed attempt leaves nothing behind — review your repository and branch selections and try again. See [AI config generation](/using-with-ai/config-generation-from-repository) for how the analysis works.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
# Agent Mode in Dev


> **Warning - Preview — in active development:** Agent mode is usable today but still evolving. Verify available endpoints by calling `GET /` on the running agent server. Some details on this page may change between Stacktape releases.


Stacktape [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) can start an HTTP API server alongside your local workloads and databases. This **agent mode** gives AI coding assistants — and any HTTP client — programmatic access to check workload status, trigger rebuilds, read log file paths, query local databases, and call AWS SDK commands, enabling automated edit-test-fix loops without manual intervention.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## When to use

Agent mode is designed for workflows where an AI coding assistant drives the edit-test-fix loop. Enable it when:

- **AI-driven development** — You're using Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or another AI coding assistant to build your application. The assistant starts `stacktape dev --agent` as a shell command, then uses the HTTP API to check status, rebuild workloads, read the log file path, query local databases, call AWS SDK commands, and stop dev mode.
- **Automated test harnesses** — You want a script to verify application behavior during development by hitting the status, env, or database endpoints.
- **Database inspection without client tools** — You need to run SQL queries, check Redis keys, scan DynamoDB items, or search OpenSearch indices against local dev databases without installing separate database clients.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## When NOT to use

- **Manual development** — If you're editing code yourself and checking results in a browser, standard [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) without `--agent` is simpler. The TUI output is optimized for human reading.
- **Production observability** — Agent mode runs locally. For deployed stacks, use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs), [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics), or the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview).
- **CI/CD pipelines** — Use [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) directly in your pipeline. Agent mode is a development-time feature.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## Starting agent mode

Add the `--agent` flag to the [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) command to start the HTTP API server alongside your workloads.

```bash
stacktape dev --agent --agentPort 9900 --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

| Flag            | Description                                                                              |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--agent`       | Enables the agent HTTP API server alongside dev mode                                     |
| `--agentPort`   | Port for the agent HTTP server                                                           |
| `--stage`       | Stage used for dev mode and the `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` directory                 |
| `--region`      | AWS region used by dev mode and as the default for `/aws/sdk` when `region` is omitted   |
| `--resources`   | Which workloads to run (`all` or comma-separated names)                                  |
| `--freshDb`     | Reset local database data on startup                                                     |

Once ready, Stacktape prints the agent URL and a summary of available endpoints. Local database data persists in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` between runs — use `--freshDb` to wipe it for a clean slate.


> **Warning - Keep the agent port private:** The agent HTTP API has no application-level authentication and the server does not explicitly restrict its listener to the loopback interface. Do not expose the port through a public interface, port forward, tunnel, or permissive container/network configuration. Anyone who can reach it may be able to rebuild workloads, query local data, stop the session, or call AWS APIs with the dev agent's credentials.


> **Tip:** AI coding assistants can call `GET /` on the agent server to receive a full endpoint listing dynamically. Use `GET /?compact=true` for a shorter LLM-oriented response — it includes the current phase, workload names, available local resources with their primary query/schema endpoints, core action templates (rebuild, logs, env, aws, stop), and a pointer to `GET /` for full docs.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## Response format

Every agent endpoint wraps its result in a consistent JSON envelope so clients can handle success and error uniformly.

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "message": "OK",
  "data": {}
}
```

| Field     | Description                                                                          |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `v`       | Envelope version (currently `"1.0"`)                                                 |
| `ok`      | `true` on success, `false` on error                                                  |
| `code`    | Machine-readable status. Common values include `OK`, `NOT_FOUND`, `VALIDATION_ERROR`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`, `ALREADY_EXISTS`, `AUTH_ERROR`, and `READ_ONLY_VIOLATION` |
| `message` | Human-readable description (optional — most responses include it, but not all)       |
| `data`    | Endpoint-specific payload (optional — present when the endpoint returns structured data) |

Many not-found and validation errors include contextual hints in `data`, such as an `available` array of valid resource names or a `hint` string describing expected input. For example, referencing a non-existent workload returns the list of available workloads in `data.available` and a usage hint in `data.hint`. This makes it easy for AI agents to self-correct without extra calls.

Agent endpoints return a JSON envelope with `v`, `ok`, and `code` on every response; most successful responses also include `message` and endpoint-specific `data`. Response examples throughout this page may omit envelope fields like `v` for brevity.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content: ## Core endpoints

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Status

The `/status` endpoint reports the current agent phase and a map of workload names to their local URLs (if running) or status strings. AI agents should poll this endpoint after starting dev mode and wait for `"ready"` before testing workload URLs.

```bash
curl http://localhost:9900/status
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "phase": "ready",
    "ready": true,
    "workloads": {
      "api": "http://localhost:3000",
      "worker": "running"
    },
    "pid": 12345
  }
}
```

The `phase` value is one of `starting`, `ready`, `rebuilding`, `stopping`, or `stopped`. In the current server code, `/status` moves phase from `starting` to `ready` once workloads are running or errored, and `/stop` moves phase to `stopping`. The `ready` field becomes `true` when there is at least one workload and every workload has reached `running` or `error` status.

For detailed information including uptime, per-workload type/port/error data, local resource status, and the log file path, use verbose mode.

```bash
curl "http://localhost:9900/status?verbose=true"
```

The verbose response replaces the workload string map with an array of objects containing `name`, `type`, `status`, `url`, `port`, and `error` fields, plus a `localResources` array, `uptime` in seconds, and the `logFile` path. Workload `status` is one of `pending`, `starting`, `running`, `error`, or `stopped`. Local resource status uses the same values.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Logs

The `/logs` endpoint returns the path to the JSONL log file on disk. Logs are **not** streamed through the HTTP response — AI agents should read the file directly using standard tools like `tail`, `grep`, or `jq`.

```bash
curl http://localhost:9900/logs
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "logFile": ".stacktape/dev-data/dev/9900-logs.txt",
    "format": "jsonl",
    "hint": "Use standard tools: tail -n 50 <logFile> | jq ."
  }
}
```

Each line in the log file is a JSON object with these fields:

| Field    | Example                      | Description                           |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `ts`     | `"2025-03-15T14:30:15Z"`    | ISO timestamp                         |
| `source` | `"api"`                      | Workload name that produced the log   |
| `level`  | `"info"`, `"warn"`, `"error"` | Severity level                      |
| `msg`    | `"Server started on :3000"`  | Log message content                   |

View the last 50 lines:

```bash
tail -n 50 .stacktape/dev-data/dev/9900-logs.txt
```

Filter for errors only:

```bash
grep '"level":"error"' .stacktape/dev-data/dev/9900-logs.txt
```

Filter by a specific workload:

```bash
grep '"source":"api"' .stacktape/dev-data/dev/9900-logs.txt
```

This file-based approach is intentional — AI coding assistants already have file-reading tools, and `tail -f` provides real-time streaming without polling overhead.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Environment variables

The `/env/{workload}` endpoint returns the environment variables available to a specific workload. For Lambda functions, variables are fetched from the deployed AWS function configuration. For other workload types whose env vars are tracked by dev mode (currently container, hosting-bucket, and nextjs-web workloads), variables are read from the local runner state.

```bash
curl http://localhost:9900/env/api
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "workload": "api",
    "type": "function",
    "source": "aws",
    "envVars": {
      "STP_NOTES_TABLE_TABLE_NAME": "my-project-dev-notesTable",
      "AWS_REGION": "eu-west-1"
    },
    "count": 2
  }
}
```

This endpoint is useful for debugging [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) wiring. If an expected `STP_*` variable is missing, the workload's `connectTo` array likely doesn't reference the target resource. The response also includes the `source` field — `"aws"` for Lambda functions (fetched from the deployed function configuration) or `"local"` for other tracked workload types (currently container, hosting-bucket, and nextjs-web workloads, read from the local runner state).

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Rebuild

After editing application code, trigger a workload rebuild to pick up the changes. Rebuilding a specific workload is faster than rebuilding all of them — AI agents should target only the workload whose code changed.

Rebuild a specific workload:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/rebuild/api
```

Rebuild all workloads at once:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/rebuild/all
```

If a workload is currently in the `starting` state (mid-rebuild), the server rejects the request with an error message. The rebuild-all endpoint also rejects if any workload is mid-rebuild, listing the names of the workloads that are still starting.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Liveness check

`GET /health` returns the current agent phase and can be used as a simple liveness check. Unlike `/status`, `/health` does not include workloads or local resources — it only returns `ok` and the current agent `phase` inside the standard envelope. Use `/status` for full workload details.

```bash
curl http://localhost:9900/health
```

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Resource health checks

Check the health of a specific local resource (database, cache). The agent monitors local resources automatically, but this endpoint triggers an immediate check and returns the result.

```bash
curl http://localhost:9900/health/myDb
```

The response includes `name`, `type`, `port`, `host`, and the `status` value returned by the local health monitor. If the resource name doesn't match any running local resource, the error response includes an `available` array listing valid resource names.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Stop

Gracefully shut down dev mode, all workloads, and all local resources.

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/stop
```

Calling stop when the agent is already stopping or stopped returns success without side effects.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## Database endpoints

Agent mode exposes HTTP endpoints for local resource instances started by dev mode. The current server has typed handlers for PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Redis, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch resources, so AI agents can inspect schemas, run queries, and verify data without installing separate database client tools. `GET /` lists only the database endpoint groups for local resources currently running in this dev session. If a resource is not running or has a different local type, the endpoint returns an error with available resource names where applicable.

The `{name}` path parameter in every database endpoint matches the resource name in your Stacktape configuration. If you reference a name that doesn't exist, the error response includes an `available` array listing the valid resource names.


> **Warning:** The PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Redis command/query endpoints accept an optional `confirm` field. The startup documentation warns that destructive operations require `{"confirm": true}` in the request body — without it, the request is rejected. The DynamoDB and OpenSearch delete handlers do not accept a `confirm` parameter; they require the key or document identifier fields shown below.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### PostgreSQL

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) with a PostgreSQL engine in your Stacktape configuration.

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/postgres/myDb/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"sql": "SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10"}'
```

| Endpoint                          | Method | Description                    | Parameters                            |
| --------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `/postgres/{name}/query`          | POST   | Execute SQL                    | `{sql, limit?, timeout?, confirm?}`   |
| `/postgres/{name}/schema`         | GET    | Column types and constraints   | `?tables=t1,t2` (optional filter)     |
| `/postgres/{name}/tables`         | GET    | List all tables                |                                       |
| `/postgres/{name}/explain`        | POST   | Query execution plan           | `{sql, analyze?}`                     |
| `/postgres/{name}/indexes`        | GET    | Index definitions              | `?table=name` (optional filter)       |
| `/postgres/{name}/stats`          | GET    | Table statistics               | `?table=name` (optional filter)       |
| `/postgres/{name}/sample`         | GET    | Sample rows from a table       | `?table=name&limit=5`                 |

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### MySQL

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) with a MySQL or MariaDB engine in your Stacktape configuration. The endpoint path uses `/mysql/` for both MySQL and MariaDB resources.

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/mysql/myDb/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"sql": "SHOW TABLES"}'
```

| Endpoint                        | Method | Description                    | Parameters                                             |
| ------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `/mysql/{name}/query`           | POST   | Execute SQL                    | `{sql, limit?, timeout?, confirm?}`                    |
| `/mysql/{name}/schema`          | GET    | Column types and constraints   | `?tables=t1,t2` (optional filter)                      |
| `/mysql/{name}/tables`          | GET    | List all tables                |                                                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/explain`         | POST   | Query execution plan           | `{sql, format?}` (format: `"traditional"`, `"json"`, or `"tree"`) |
| `/mysql/{name}/indexes`         | GET    | Index definitions              | `?table=name` (optional filter)                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/stats`           | GET    | Table statistics               | `?table=name` (optional filter)                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/sample`          | GET    | Sample rows from a table       | `?table=name&limit=5`                                  |

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Redis

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [Redis cluster](/resources/databases/redis) in your Stacktape configuration. The `cmd` field accepts a Redis command as a single string (e.g. `"GET mykey"`, `"SET user:1 '{\"name\":\"Alice\"}'"`).

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/redis/myCache/command \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"cmd": "GET session:user123"}'
```

| Endpoint                       | Method | Description                  | Parameters                       |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `/redis/{name}/command`        | POST   | Execute any Redis command    | `{cmd, confirm?}`               |
| `/redis/{name}/keys`           | GET    | List keys matching pattern   | `?pattern=*&limit=100`          |
| `/redis/{name}/get`            | GET    | Get value by key             | `?key=name`                     |
| `/redis/{name}/ttl`            | GET    | Get TTL for a key            | `?key=name`                     |
| `/redis/{name}/info`           | GET    | Server info                  | `?section=memory` (optional)    |
| `/redis/{name}/type`           | GET    | Get type of a key            | `?key=name`                     |

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### DynamoDB

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) in your Stacktape configuration. Key parameters (`pk`, `sk`) are objects mapping attribute names to values — for example, `{"userId": "123"}`.

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/dynamodb/notesTable/scan \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"limit": 10}'
```

| Endpoint                           | Method | Description                  | Parameters                                    |
| ---------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/query`           | POST   | Query by partition/sort key  | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?, index?, limit?}`       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/scan`            | POST   | Full table scan              | `{filter?, limit?}`                           |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/get`             | POST   | Get single item              | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?}`                       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/put`             | POST   | Put an item                  | `{item: {...}}`                               |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/delete`          | POST   | Delete an item               | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?}`                       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/schema`          | GET    | Table key schema and indexes |                                                |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/sample`          | GET    | Sample items                 | `?limit=5`                                    |

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### OpenSearch

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for an [OpenSearch domain](/resources/databases/opensearch) in your Stacktape configuration. Query bodies follow standard OpenSearch query DSL.

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/opensearch/searchDomain/search \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": {"match": {"title": "serverless"}}, "limit": 10}'
```

| Endpoint                             | Method | Description                  | Parameters                           |
| ------------------------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `/opensearch/{name}/search`          | POST   | Search documents             | `{query: {...}, index?, limit?}`     |
| `/opensearch/{name}/get`             | GET    | Get document by ID           | `?index=idx&id=docid`               |
| `/opensearch/{name}/put`             | POST   | Index a document             | `{index, id?, doc: {...}}`           |
| `/opensearch/{name}/delete`          | POST   | Delete a document            | `{index, id}`                        |
| `/opensearch/{name}/indices`         | GET    | List all indices             |                                      |
| `/opensearch/{name}/mapping`         | GET    | Get index mapping            | `?index=idx`                         |
| `/opensearch/{name}/analyze`         | POST   | Analyze text with tokenizer  | `{text, analyzer?, index?}`          |
| `/opensearch/{name}/count`           | GET    | Count documents              | `?index=idx` (optional)              |

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## AWS SDK access

Agent mode provides direct access to AWS SDK commands through the `/aws/sdk` endpoint. The endpoint uses credentials returned by `getDevAgentCredentials()` — dev agent role credentials scoped to the stack, with a fallback to user credentials. If no usable access key and secret key are returned, the request fails with an error. The startup message describes this access as scoped to stack resources via IAM role.

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9900/aws/sdk \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"service": "lambda", "command": "ListFunctions", "input": {"MaxItems": 10}}'
```

The request body accepts `service` (required), `command` (required), `input` (optional, defaults to `{}`), and `region` (optional, defaults to the dev mode region). If `service` or `command` is missing, the agent returns a validation error with a hint showing the expected request shape.

To list all supported services and example commands:

```bash
curl http://localhost:9900/aws/sdk/services
```

`GET /aws/sdk/services` returns a successful envelope whose payload includes the supported services from `getSupportedServices()`. In the current implementation, the services payload is nested under `data.data` in the response. Use the running endpoint response as the authoritative shape and list of valid `service` values before constructing `/aws/sdk` calls. The service list in the startup message and on this page is a summary; the endpoint response is always up to date.

Common AWS SDK calls for AI agents:

| Use case                  | Service            | Command              | Example input                                                  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Read Lambda logs          | `logs`             | `FilterLogEvents`    | `{"logGroupName": "/aws/lambda/fn", "filterPattern": "ERROR"}` |
| Scan a DynamoDB table     | `dynamodb`         | `Scan`               | `{"TableName": "tbl", "Limit": 10}`                           |
| List S3 objects           | `s3`               | `ListObjectsV2`      | `{"Bucket": "bkt", "Prefix": "uploads/"}`                     |
| Invoke a Lambda           | `lambda`           | `Invoke`             | `{"FunctionName": "fn", "Payload": "{}"}`                     |
| Describe a stack          | `cloudformation`   | `DescribeStacks`     | `{"StackName": "my-stack"}`                                    |


> **Info:** The startup message lists supported `service` identifiers: `lambda`, `dynamodb`, `s3`, `logs`, `cloudformation`, `cloudwatch`, `sqs`, `sns`, `sfn`, `eventbridge`, `secretsmanager`, `ssm`, `sts`, `iam`, `ec2`, `ecs`, `ecr`, `rds`, `ses`, `cognito`, `apigatewayv2`, `xray`, `kinesis`, `firehose`, and more. Call `GET /aws/sdk/services` on the running agent for the complete, up-to-date list.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## Typical AI agent workflow

The core value of agent mode is the **automated feedback loop**: an AI agent writes code, checks if it works, reads any errors, fixes them, and rebuilds — all without human intervention.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## Flow
1. **Write config**: AI writes or edits stacktape.ts based on your requirements
2. **Start agent mode**: AI runs stacktape dev --agent to boot workloads and databases
3. **Write application code**: AI implements handlers, services, and frontend code
4. **Rebuild and test**: AI calls POST /rebuild/{name}, checks status, reads logs, queries databases
5. **Fix and iterate**: AI reads error logs, fixes code, rebuilds — repeating until everything works
6. **Deploy**: Once working locally, AI deploys to AWS with stacktape deploy

title: Agent Mode in Dev
Agent Mode in Dev
content:
### Tips for AI agent integrations

- **Poll status before testing** — Wait for `"phase": "ready"` before making requests to workload URLs. Workloads may still be compiling during the `starting` phase.
- **Use compact docs** — Call `GET /?compact=true` at the start of a session to discover available endpoints with minimal token usage. The full `GET /` listing is more detailed but token-heavy.
- **Rebuild selectively** — `POST /rebuild/{name}` rebuilds only the named workload. Use it instead of `/rebuild/all` when you changed code in a single workload.
- **Check env vars early** — `GET /env/{workload}` reveals whether [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) is wired correctly before you start debugging application code.
- **Read logs from the file** — The `/logs` endpoint returns a file path. Use `tail`, `grep`, or `jq` to filter the JSONL log file. Use `tail -f` for real-time streaming.
- **Inspect schemas before writing queries** — Call the `/schema` or `/tables` endpoint to discover table and column names before writing SQL or DynamoDB queries.
- **Use database endpoints for verification** — After writing data through your API, query the database directly to confirm it was stored correctly.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## MCP server integration

For MCP-based assistant setup, see the [Stacktape MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) page. If your AI assistant supports the Model Context Protocol (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf), the MCP server provides a higher-level integration layer. Agent mode's HTTP API is the lower-level alternative that works with any tool capable of making HTTP requests.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content:
## Security

Stacktape advertises the agent URL as `http://localhost:{port}`. The server sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null` and returns `403` for OPTIONS preflight requests. The implementation comments describe this as blocking browser-based cross-origin requests while keeping curl, scripts, and local tools usable.

These CORS controls are not authentication. The HTTP server listens on the configured port without an explicit loopback-only host binding, so use host firewall and network settings to keep the port local and trusted.

The `/aws/sdk` endpoint uses credentials returned by `getDevAgentCredentials()`. If no access key and secret key are available, the endpoint returns an error (`AWS credentials not available`). The startup message describes this access as scoped to stack resources via IAM role. Treat the endpoint as having whatever permissions those credentials grant — avoid exposing the agent port to untrusted networks.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
content: ## FAQ

title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Should I use agent mode or the Stacktape MCP server?
content:
### Should I use agent mode or the Stacktape MCP server?

Both work with assistants like Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf. Agent mode is a plain HTTP API that any tool can call with `curl` or HTTP libraries — no protocol integration needed, so it suits custom tooling or any client that can make HTTP requests. The [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) uses the Model Context Protocol standard that those assistants support natively, providing a more integrated, higher-level layer. If your AI tool supports MCP, prefer the MCP server; reach for agent mode when you need raw HTTP access.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: What databases can I query through the agent API?
content:
### What databases can I query through the agent API?

Agent mode exposes typed HTTP endpoints for five local resource types started by dev mode — PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Redis, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch — so agents can inspect schemas, run queries, and verify data without installing separate database client tools. Each type has its own endpoint group (SQL engines get `query`/`schema`/`tables`/`explain`/`indexes`/`stats`/`sample`, plus key-value and document operations for Redis, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch). `GET /` lists only the endpoint groups for resources currently running in the session.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Is my data persisted between agent mode sessions?
content:
### Is my data persisted between agent mode sessions?

Yes. The startup message confirms local database data is stored in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` and survives restarts. Use the `--freshDb` flag when starting dev mode to reset all local databases to a clean state.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Are destructive database operations safe during AI sessions?
content:
### Are destructive database operations safe during AI sessions?

The PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Redis query/command endpoints accept an optional `confirm` field. The startup documentation warns that destructive operations require `{"confirm": true}` — without it, the request is rejected. DynamoDB and OpenSearch delete handlers do not accept a `confirm` parameter; they require the key or document identifier fields directly.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: What happens if a workload fails to start?
content:
### What happens if a workload fails to start?

The agent server keeps running even if individual workloads fail. The `/status` endpoint reports per-workload status — in verbose mode, each workload includes `status`, `url`, `port`, and `error` fields. AI agents can read the error, fix the code, and call `POST /rebuild/{name}` to retry without restarting the entire dev session.

title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Why does an `/aws/sdk` call fail or return access-denied?
content:
### Why does an `/aws/sdk` call fail or return access-denied?

The `/aws/sdk` endpoint runs against dev agent credentials, which the source describes as scoped to the stack's IAM role (falling back to user credentials). Those credentials determine what resources are reachable — a call can fail with `AWS credentials not available` if no usable key pair is returned, or with an access-denied error if the role lacks permission for that resource. The endpoint supports a broad set of services (`lambda`, `dynamodb`, `s3`, `logs`, `cloudformation`, `sqs`, `sns`, `sfn`, and more); call `GET /aws/sdk/services` for the authoritative, up-to-date list of valid `service` values before constructing a call.

title: AI Coding Assistant Integrations
content:
# AI Coding Assistant Integrations


> **Warning:** **Preview — in active development.** The Stacktape MCP server is under active development. Setup and behavior may change between Stacktape CLI versions. Expect improvements and possible breaking changes.


Stacktape integrates with AI coding assistants through the [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). The [`stacktape mcp:add`](/cli/mcp-add) command configures Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, OpenAI Codex, and OpenCode to launch Stacktape's local MCP server. The generated config tells the assistant to run `stacktape mcp` as a local MCP server process.

title: AI Coding Assistant Integrations
content:
## When to use

Use the MCP integration when your AI coding assistant supports MCP and you want it to launch Stacktape's local MCP server directly from the editor. See the [MCP server setup](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) page for the current tool list and server behavior. The integration is most valuable when you want a tighter feedback loop between asking questions in your assistant and taking action on your Stacktape project.

title: AI Coding Assistant Integrations
content:
## When NOT to use

Skip MCP setup if you prefer running Stacktape commands in a terminal, or if your AI client does not support MCP. For operations not covered by the MCP server, use the [CLI](/cli/deploy) directly. See [MCP server setup](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) for the current tool list.

title: AI Coding Assistant Integrations
content:
## Supported assistants

The [`stacktape mcp:add`](/cli/mcp-add) command checks known config-file paths and writes the correct MCP configuration for the clients you select. Six AI coding assistants are supported:

| Assistant | Config format | Root key | Project config path | Global config path |
|-----------|--------------|----------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Claude Code | JSON | `mcpServers` | `.mcp.json` | `~/.claude.json` |
| Cursor | JSON | `mcpServers` | `.cursor/mcp.json` | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| VS Code / GitHub Copilot | JSON | `servers` | `.vscode/mcp.json` | Platform-specific `User/mcp.json` |
| Windsurf | JSON | `mcpServers` | `.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json` | `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json` |
| OpenAI Codex | TOML | `mcp_servers` | `.codex/config.toml` | `~/.codex/config.toml` |
| OpenCode | JSON/JSONC | `mcp` | `opencode.jsonc` or `.opencode/config.json` | Platform-specific (see below) |

VS Code global paths vary by platform: on Windows `%APPDATA%\Code\User\mcp.json`, on macOS `~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/mcp.json`, on Linux `~/.config/Code/User/mcp.json`.

Windsurf global path resolves to the user's home directory on all platforms: `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json` (on Windows, `%USERPROFILE%\.codeium\windsurf\mcp_config.json`).

OpenCode global paths vary by platform: on Windows `%APPDATA%\opencode\opencode.jsonc` or `%APPDATA%\opencode\config.json`; on macOS and Linux `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`, `~/.config/opencode/config.json`, or `~/.opencode/config.json`.

Generated configs launch `stacktape mcp` locally. Claude Code, Cursor, and VS Code configs explicitly set `type: 'stdio'`; Windsurf omits the type field; OpenCode uses `type: 'local'` with the command as an array; Codex uses TOML with no type field. Other MCP-compatible clients may work if they can launch a local command with arguments and environment variables, but `mcp:add` only writes configs for the six listed clients.

title: AI Coding Assistant Integrations
content:
## One-command setup

The [`stacktape mcp:add`](/cli/mcp-add) command configures Stacktape MCP for one or more supported AI coding assistants in a single invocation.
